d: illegal gain from a position of power, such as bribes
ex: Years of graft left the city's roads in terrible condition.

d: to hide the truth about a serious mistake or crime
ex: Officials tried to cover up the missing money.

d: forcing someone to act by threatening to reveal a secret
ex: The clerk used blackmail to force the supplier to pay him.

d: getting money by force or threats
ex: The officer was charged with extortion for demanding cash from shop owners.

d: unfair support given to one person or group
ex: The tender was cancelled because of favouritism towards one firm.

d: giving jobs or favours to your own relatives
ex: The director's nepotism meant three cousins joined the department.

d: giving jobs or contracts to friends without regard to ability
ex: Cronyism meant the contract went to the mayor's old school friend.

d: giving jobs or benefits in return for loyalty or support
ex: Political patronage filled the agency with unqualified staff.

ar: عمولة غير مشروعة، رشوة مقابل صفقة
d: an illegal payment to someone who helped arrange a deal
ex: The engineer received a kickback for approving the contract.

d: to steal money that you were trusted to look after
ex: The treasurer embezzled thousands from the charity.

d: the crime of stealing money that you were trusted to manage
ex: The cashier was convicted of embezzlement.

d: to take money or property meant for one purpose and use it for another
ex: He misappropriated funds meant for a village school.

d: the act of using money or property dishonestly for a different purpose
ex: The misappropriation of aid money shocked the donors.

d: to change a document or record to make it false
ex: The accountant falsified the figures in the annual report.

d: the act of changing documents or records to make them false
ex: The falsification of invoices hid the missing payments.

d: to make a price or number higher than it should be
ex: The contractor inflated the price of the cement.

d: charging more than the real price on a bill
ex: Over-invoicing allowed the supplier to share the extra money with an official.

d: a person who is paid a salary but does not really work
ex: The audit found forty ghost workers on the council's payroll.

d: a secret fund of money used for illegal or dishonest payments
ex: Investigators found a slush fund hidden in the company's accounts.

d: money paid to someone to stop them revealing a secret
ex: The employee refused the hush money and reported the case.

d: using your connections with powerful people to get money or favours
ex: He was convicted of influence peddling after selling access to a minister.

d: pressure that unfairly makes a person take a decision
ex: The contract was cancelled because of undue influence on the committee.

d: a benefit that a person has no right to receive
ex: Offering an undue advantage to an official is a form of bribery.

d: a small illegal payment to make an official do their normal work faster
ex: A facilitation payment is still a bribe under most laws.

d: corruption by top officials involving very large sums of public money
ex: Grand corruption robs the country of money for schools and hospitals.

d: small-scale bribery in everyday dealings with officials
ex: Petty corruption happens when a clerk asks for a small payment.

d: corruption that is part of how a whole system or institution works
ex: Systemic corruption cannot be solved by punishing a few individuals.

d: very common in a place or group and hard to remove
ex: Bribery was endemic in the customs service.

d: present and spreading through every part of something
ex: A pervasive fear of retaliation stopped employees from reporting.

d: firmly established and very difficult to change
ex: Entrenched habits of secrecy slow every reform.

d: freedom from punishment for wrong acts
ex: Impunity encourages officials to repeat their abuses.

d: a strict policy of refusing to accept any wrongdoing
ex: The ministry announced zero tolerance for bribery.

d: a secret agreement between people to cheat or act illegally
ex: Collusion between bidders pushed the price up.

d: to make a secret plan with others to cheat
ex: Three firms colluded to share the contracts.

d: secretly agreeing who will win a tender and at what price
ex: Bid rigging kept prices artificially high for years.

d: a group of companies that agree to control prices
ex: The cement cartel fixed prices across the region.

d: an illegal agreement between companies to keep prices at the same level
ex: The competition authority fined the firms for price fixing.

d: a secret plan by several people to commit a crime
ex: The three officials were charged with conspiracy to commit fraud.

d: involvement in a crime together with others
ex: The report found complicity between the contractor and local officials.

d: involved in a crime or wrongdoing together with others
ex: Officials who stayed silent were complicit in the fraud.

d: hiding the illegal source of money by passing it through legal businesses
ex: The bank reported a case of money laundering to the authorities.

d: to make illegal money look legal
ex: Criminals laundered the money through a chain of small shops.

d: a company that exists only on paper and hides who really owns money
ex: Money was moved through a shell company with no staff or office.

d: a business used to hide illegal activity
ex: The front company existed only to receive the kickbacks.

d: a bank account in another country, often to avoid tax or detection
ex: He hid the bribes in an offshore account.

d: a place where taxes are very low and information is kept secret
ex: The profits were sent to a tax haven.

d: not allowed by law or by accepted rules
ex: Illicit payments were hidden as consulting fees.

d: a large increase in an official's wealth that he cannot explain legally
ex: The judge charged him with illicit enrichment because his assets were too large.

d: money or property that an official cannot show a legal source for
ex: The law allows courts to act against unexplained wealth.

d: illegal movement of money across borders
ex: Illicit financial flows drain billions from developing countries.

d: money or property obtained through criminal acts
ex: The court froze the proceeds of crime held in his name.

d: real ownership by the person who finally enjoys the profits
ex: A public register of beneficial ownership shows who really owns a company.

d: the real person who owns or controls a company and receives its profits
ex: The beneficial owner was a minister's son.

d: a person with an important public job who needs extra checks by banks
ex: Banks must check every account of a politically exposed person closely.

d: banking rules that require identity checks on customers
ex: Know your customer rules help banks spot dirty money.

d: a money transfer that seems linked to crime
ex: The bank filed a report on a suspicious transaction.

d: an official order that stops a person from using their property
ex: The court ordered an asset freeze on all his accounts.

d: to take property officially as a punishment or for evidence
ex: Police confiscated the cash found in his car.

d: the official taking of property by the state
ex: Confiscation of the luxury villa was part of the sentence.

d: losing property as a legal punishment
ex: Forfeiture of his house was ordered by the court.

d: getting stolen public money or property back, often from abroad
ex: Asset recovery returned millions to the national treasury.

d: cooperation between countries in investigations and trials
ex: Mutual legal assistance helped investigators trace the bank accounts abroad.

d: serious crime carried out by well-planned criminal groups
ex: Organised crime groups often depend on corrupt officials.

d: involving more than one country
ex: Corruption is often a transnational crime involving banks abroad.

d: movement of people between public posts and private companies they regulated
ex: The revolving door raises questions about conflicts of interest.

d: trying to influence officials or lawmakers on behalf of a group
ex: Rules on lobbying must be public and clear.

d: a system of government where leaders steal national wealth
ex: Kleptocracy leaves the population poor while a few leaders grow rich.

d: when private interests control public decisions for their own benefit
ex: State capture happens when companies buy laws and public jobs.

d: an official body created to prevent and investigate corruption
ex: The anti-corruption agency opened an investigation into the contract.

d: using political influence to gain wealth without producing anything new
